}}'''Henry James Priestley''' (10 April 1883 – 26 February 1932) was the first Professor of Mathematics at the [[University of Queensland]].

== Education ==
Henry James Priestley was born in [[Crouch Hill]], London. He was educated at Mill Hill School and [[Jesus College, Cambridge|Jesus College]], University of Cambridge, where he gained his B.A. with honours first class (second division).<ref name="adb.anu.edu.au">[https://adb.anu.edu.au/biography/priestley-henry-james-8115 Biography – Henry James Priestley – Australian Dictionary of Biography<!-- Bot generated title -->]</ref> He was fifth [[Wrangler (University of Cambridge)|wrangler]] in the [[Mathematical Tripos]] of 1905. In 1909 he received his M.A. from Cambridge.<ref>{{cite news|url = https://nla.gov.au/nla.news-article181253995|title = 26 February 1932-Professor Priestley|last = H.W.D.|date = 26 February 1932|work = The Telegraph (Brisbane, Qld): 26 February 1932: 19|access-date = 12 November 2015|via = National Library of Australia}}</ref><ref name=":1" />

== Career ==
After graduating from Cambridge, Priestley lectured in mathematics at the Victoria University of Manchester (now [[University of Manchester]]) in 1907.<ref>{{cite web|title = Physics in Australia to 1945 – PRIESTLEY, Henry James|url = https://www.asap.unimelb.edu.au/bsparcs/physics/P001784p.htm|website = www.asap.unimelb.edu.au|access-date = 2015-11-12}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite book|title = Henry Priestley in Vivant Professores|last = Gregory|first = Helen|publisher = University of Queensland Library|year = 1987|isbn = 0-908471-09-2|url = https://espace.library.uq.edu.au/view/UQ:151381/flop_7.pdf|pages = 118–120}}</ref> He married Margery Hewitt in 1909 in London. In 1910, The [[University of Queensland]], in Brisbane, Australia advertised extensively, four new professor positions in the newly formed University. After Professor [[Ernest Rutherford]] of the University of Manchester declined it, Priestley's application was considered and voted favourably upon.<ref name=":0">{{cite web|url = http://www.uq.edu.au/crossroads/Archives/Vol%205/Issue%202%202011/Vol5Iss211%20-%208.Mainstone%20(p.45-55).pdf|title = The Selection of Physics as a Foundation Discipline at The University of Queensland|date = 2011|access-date = 12 November 2015|website = Crossroads archives. 5(2) :45–55.|publisher = University of Queensland|last = Mainstone|first = John|archive-date = 3 March 2016|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20160303221025/http://www.uq.edu.au/crossroads/Archives/Vol%205/Issue%202%202011/Vol5Iss211%20-%208.Mainstone%20(p.45-55).pdf|url-status = dead}}</ref> Priestley would become Professor of mathematics and physics. He and his wife arrived in Brisbane in 1911, on the same boat as his colleague Professor [[John Lundie Michie]]. However Priestley soon realised he couldn't teach all the necessary subjects alone, and so [[Thomas Parnell (scientist)|Thomas Parnell]], who was teaching at [[the University of Melbourne]], found his application to lecture in physics successful.<ref name=":0" /> By 1919 the senate of the University decided to create separate departments of mathematics and physics. Priestley was offered either chair and chose mathematics.<ref name="adb.anu.edu.au"/> Thomas Parnell was offered the physics chair.

In 1912 Priestley became a member of the [[London Mathematical Society]] and subsequently published papers in its proceedings and in other journals, mainly in the areas of applied mathematics and [[mathematical physics]]. He believed the University would not succeed unless its academics published extensively to improve its reputation.<ref name=":1" /> Priestley had considerable influence on university affairs, and despaired at the state of the buildings and library.<ref name=":1" /> He served as Dean of the Faculty of Science (1911–19). He was president of the Board of Faculties (later professorial board) (1922–25) and was a member of many standing committees of the senate and board.<ref name="adb.anu.edu.au"/> He was a keen member of the University Musical Society. He was also a supporter of hockey at the university, his daughter later becoming a member of the women's team.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.uqhockey.com.au/wspClubHistory.aspx|title=Club History - UQ Hockey Club|website=www.uqhockey.com.au|access-date=2020-03-16}}</ref> His wife was active in the establishment of the Women's College at the University.<ref name=":1" />

A founder of the Queensland branch of the Mathematical Association of Great Britain, Priestley was its president for many years. He was President of the [[Royal Society of Queensland]] in 1923. He spoke at lecture tours throughout Queensland, notably on [[Albert Einstein|Einstein]]'s theory of relativity.<ref name="adb.anu.edu.au"/>

Priestley died on 26 February 1932 of a cerebral tumour after a long illness, survived by his wife, three sons and a daughter. His obituary was given in the newspapers by his colleague, Professor [[John Lundie Michie]].<ref>{{cite news|url = https://nla.gov.au/nla.news-article21784796|title = 27 Feb 1932 – Obituary|work = The Brisbane Courier, 27 February 1932: 19.|access-date = 12 November 2015|via = National Library of Australia}}</ref>

His eldest son Henry Thomas Priestley, was a key advocate for the establishment of Townsville University College (now [[James Cook University]]) in 1960.<ref name="adb.anu.edu.au"/>

== Legacy ==
A major building at the University of Queensland bears his name.<ref name=":1" />
